newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU decision seen more than just a numbers game.
newsitem.headline: EMU decision seen more than just a numbers game.

text.p: The fate of a common European currency, and all of the wider political implications of monetary union, hinges on more than a few fractions of a percentage point, analysts and EU officials say.
In recent weeks financial markets have shown a near manic obsession with Maastricht treaty's deficit criteria for monetary union and how strictly they will be applied.
Analysts say the intensity of this focus may explain why sentiment towards economic and monetary union has swung so wildly in the past few months, often at odds with underlying economic fundamentals.

While EU policy-makers are somewhat to blame for fuelling speculation over how the criteria will be read, the sharp reaction to every twist and turn in this story suggests many investors view the project as an all or nothing event.
"The perception of markets is not that we are in a continuous spectrum but that we are in a kind of dichotomous world of yes or no," said one senior EU official.
"The real world is a bit less dichotomous."

Judging by the latest drama over whether Germany is edging away from a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty's deficit criteria one might conclude that EMU is now definitely on course as planned for 1999 and that it will include a large number of the EU's 15 members.
The optimism is such that even countries like Italy have benefitted, this despite a 1997 mini-budget which has been criticised for too many one-off measures.
Utlimately, the judgment on a country's fitness for EMU will depend on more than whether they have their public finances under control in 1997.

As EU Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy pointed out at a meeting of EU finance ministers at the weekend, 1998 budget estimates will be used to determine whether fiscal consolidation is "sustainable."
Peter Praet, economist at Generale Bank in Brussels, reckons that the sustainability question could ironically open the door to a much larger bloc of entrants.
Those with budget deficits not quite up to scratch in 1997 might argue that their outlook for 1998 is much better given favourable assumptions on growth and interest rates.
Other analysts note that the markets' renewed optimism in EMU may stem from the belief that it is largely a political project.
"Whether in reality there has been any change in Germany meeting the convergence criteria is a moot point," says Martin Brookes, economist at Goldman Sachs in London.

"I think what we've seen in the past week is a new injection of political will in the project," he added, with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to stand for re-election in 1998 seen as a pivotal event.
Notwithstanding Germany's hardline stance on the criteria, there is a strong belief among experts that the decision on EMU membership will retain some degree of flexibility.
To be sure, there are limits on how much room for maneouvre EU leaders have.
Germany would face an immense challenge if its 1997 budget deficit registered 3.5 percent of GDP, rather than three percent as prescribed in the Maastyricht treaty.
Such an outcome would make it more difficult to exclude countries whose deficits ranged between 3.5 and 4.0 percent of total output.
Objectively, analysts say the challenge for most countries is to ensure that they come reasonably close to the three percent target.

Given the political fallout and economic turbulence that would arise from not proceeding with EMU on schedule, it seems inconceivable to many that the project would be postponed because of a slight overshoot of the Maastricht target.
